title: Korach: the man who went home (Sanhedrin 109b)
hook: On ben Peleth vanishes from the rebellion; the Talmud says his wife talked him out of it

segments.voice: Yesterday, attacked in front of everyone, Moses fell on his face before he said a word. Your line was fall silent first. Did you manage one breath before a reply? Day four hundred fifty-four.

Read the first verse of the Korach story slowly and you'll find a roll call. Korach. Dathan and Abiram. And one more: On, the son of Peleth. He's right there at the start of the rebellion, named with the leaders. Then he's gone. When the trouble comes to its terrible end, Korach, Dathan and Abiram are all named again. On never appears again, anywhere in the Bible. Readers noticed the gap a long time ago. What happened to the fourth man? The Talmud has an answer, and it's a story about a kitchen-table conversation.
screen: `A ROLL CALL OF REBELS.` → `ON, THE SON OF PELETH.` → `THEN HE'S GONE.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, and here it is in paraphrase. On's wife asks him a simple question. What do you get out of this? If Moses stays the leader, you're a follower. If Korach becomes the leader, you're still a follower. On admits she's right, but says he's stuck: he was in the meeting, he gave his word, they're counting on him. So she says, in effect, leave it to me. She gives him wine, he falls asleep inside the tent, and she sits at the entrance, in a way that makes the men coming to fetch him turn back. By the time he wakes, the rebellion is over, and he's alive. The Talmud reads a verse from Proverbs over the scene: every wise woman builds her house, but the foolish one tears it down with her own hands. The wise woman is On's wife. And the foolish one? The same passage says Korach's wife egged him on, feeding his resentment of Moses. So two homes, two conversations, two endings. A few things are worth noticing. The Torah itself says nothing about any of this; the Talmud is answering a silence in the text. Her argument isn't about who's right. It's about him: this fight isn't yours, and it won't give you what you think. And On's problem, but I already gave my word, is one plenty of people know. Sometimes the bravest thing is letting someone who loves you talk you down from a fight you joined too fast.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU GET OUT OF THIS?` · `SHE SITS AT THE TENT'S ENTRANCE.` · `A WISE WOMAN BUILDS HER HOUSE.` · `THE TORAH IS SILENT; THE TALMUD ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let someone talk you down. Settle, and breathe. Think of the person in your life who's good at asking, what do you actually get out of this? A partner, a friend, a sibling, an old teacher. Picture their face. Now think of one fight you're in, or one you're tempted to join. Imagine telling them about it. What would they ask? Let the question sit with you, without defending yourself. If you're grateful for that person, let yourself feel it. Breathe until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Korach. The rebellion that started with four named men, and ended, the Talmud says, with one of them asleep safely at home.
Your line: she saved him. Today, before you dig in on something, ask one person you trust what they think, and really listen. Day four hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: The story of On ben Peleth and his wife is a well-known Talmudic teaching that is often told when the portion of Korach is read in synagogue in early summer.

match.prompt: who did what — tap the pairs.
pairs: named at the start, then gone

myth: the Torah tells us On's wife saved him
the Torah only names On once. the story of his wife comes from the Talmud, Sanhedrin 109b.
On's wife argued that he'd be a follower either way
if Moses leads, you follow; if Korach leads, you still follow.
On is named again when the rebellion ends
Korach, Dathan and Abiram are named again. On never reappears.

fork.setup: you're On. you joined the rebels, you gave your word, and your wife says this fight will get you nothing. what do you do?
options: keep your word to the rebels.
let her handle it, and stay home.
go to Moses and switch sides loudly.
fork.reveal: in the Talmud's story, he stays home and sleeps while she keeps the rebels away from the tent. he lives; the rebellion doesn't.

original.note: Hebrew: On, son of Peleth, named in Numbers 16:1 and never again.

trapdoor: what you thought: one more name in a list of rebels.
what it means: a man who joined the rebellion and quietly disappeared from it.
what a scholar hears: Sanhedrin 109b fills the gap with his wife's intervention, reading Proverbs 14:1 over her: the wise woman builds her house, the foolish one (Korach's wife) tears it down.

notes: Sanhedrin 109b–110a (attributed to Rav): On's wife's argument, the wine, sitting at the tent entrance with her hair uncovered so the rebels turned back; Korach's wife's provocation. The script softens the hair detail to 'in a way that makes the men turn back'; a Keeper may prefer it stated plainly.
Confirm that On ben Peleth is not mentioned anywhere else in the Tanakh.
The Talmud applies Proverbs 14:1 to the two wives; paraphrased rather than quoted from JPS 1917 because the exact JPS wording wasn't certain.
